title: Redwood Console Walkthrough - Tracing & Debugging
summary: AE + SE demo of Redwood Console focusing on tracing, request logs, error analysis, and debugging flows. Customer asked about access patterns, RBAC/KMS, retaining request logs for audits, and how to debug model regressions. Agreed next steps: share security pack, schedule pilot benchmark, and send pricing/throughput worksheet.
next_steps: Alex to send security pack and SOC2 summary (by 2025-03-14)
Priya to share Console short screencast and request-log export example (by 2025-03-15)
Customer to provide 2 sample prompts and target latency SLOs for pilot (by 2025-03-18)
Schedule pilot kickoff with Dedicated ops if pilot is approved (tentative week of 2025-03-24)
action_items: Alex: Email SOC2/ISO summary + security pack (due 2025-03-14)
Priya: Upload 5-min Console screencast and sample exported logs (due 2025-03-15)
Samir: Share current request volume and P95 latency targets (due 2025-03-18)
Jorge: Confirm encryption/KMS questions to send to Redwood SEs (due 2025-03-17)
transcript:
00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Today Priya and I will walk through the Console tracing, request logs, and how you can debug errors end-to-end in Redwood.
00:09 Emma Walker: Hi! Thanks. We wanted to focus on observability — especially how we would triage errors during peak loads.
00:16 Priya Kapoor: Great, we'll start with the tracing view. Quick note — I'll be sharing my screen. The view shows a request timeline, per-token latency and the model variant used.
00:28 Marcus Li: Sometimes the model switches to a quantized fallback; you'll see that in the trace as a different node.
00:35 Samir Patel: Sorry, quantized fallback meaning like a lower-precision variant when capacity is constrained?
00:39 Priya Kapoor: Exactly. It's a compatible model variant we route to when Dedicated pools are full or a cheaper route for non-latency-critical traffic.
00:47 Lydia Chen: How does that show up in logs? Can we filter by model variant?
00:51 Priya Kapoor: Yes — in the trace you can filter on model tag and on route. You can also group by customer tenant if you're running multi-tenant.
01:00 Alex Chen: We'll jump into a sample trace. Notice at 02:12 there's a small spike — that's a retry. The trace shows request metadata: route id, model id, sequence length, token counts, and KV-cache hits.
01:15 Emma Walker: KV cache? We usually see that spelled out to our infra folks as kay-vee cache in notes.
01:20 Marcus Li: Right, internal transcriptions vary. The Console shows cache hits/misses per prefix — it's useful to see cold-start tokens.
01:30 Samir Patel: How granular are the timestamps? We need sub-10ms resolution for P50/P95 analysis.
01:35 Priya Kapoor: We capture per-stage timings at millisecond granularity and aggregate to the dashboards. The trace view shows per-request steps with relative ms. For export we provide CSV/NDJSON with timestamps in epoch ms.
01:49 Jorge Rivera: From a security perspective, how long do logs persist and can we limit PII? We need audit logs for 12 months.
01:57 Alex Chen: Good question. By default hosted logs retain 90 days, but Dedicated/Private options allow longer retention and you control exports. For SOC2 customers we can set up a log-archive to your S3 and support 12+ months retention.
02:12 Lydia Chen: And PII — do you redact or can we push redaction rules?
02:16 Priya Kapoor: We offer configurable transformations at ingestion: regex-based redaction, tokenization, and you can route raw logs to a customer-controlled bucket if you need to run your own redaction pipeline.
02:30 Emma Walker: That would be useful. Can you show an error analysis flow — say a model returns malformed JSON and the app breaks?
02:38 Priya Kapoor: Sure. I'll trigger a demo error. You can see here the request log entry includes the prompt, the returned text, the status code, and an error field if execution failed. For structured output we also compare expected schema vs actual and flag mismatches.
02:55 Marcus Li: In the debug panel we link the failing request to a test prompt set and the eval run that covered it, so you can quickly reproduce the exact prompt-model combination.
03:05 Samir Patel: Does that mean we can run a replay? Like re-run the single request against a pinned model version?
03:10 Priya Kapoor: Yes — replays are supported for up to the retention window or the export you kept. You can replay against the same model snapshot or a candidate model to check regression. Replays will be isolated and not counted against production quotas in pilot mode.
03:25 Lydia Chen: Good. What about distributed tracing — can we correlate Redwood traces with our app traces? We use Jaeger and OpenTelemetry.
03:32 Alex Chen: We emit trace IDs in the request logs. You can propagate your trace-id header and Redwood will persist it in logs and the trace timeline, so you can join on that in your backend tracing system. We also support exporting spans via OTLP to your collector in our Private deployment.
03:50 Jorge Rivera: KMS question — where are keys stored and who has access? We need HSM-backed keys for production.
03:56 Alex Chen: For Private and Dedicated, we support customer-managed KMS keys via AWS KMS/HSM or compatible KMS. We can integrate with your key policies so only your service principals can decrypt. For hosted, we use industry-standard KMS with strict access controls and audit logs; for HSM bring-your-own is available on Dedicated.
04:15 Samir Patel: Ok, so in the trace we'd see an encryption flag?
04:18 Priya Kapoor: There's a metadata field indicating whether payloads were encrypted at rest and which KMS alias was used; it's present in the request metadata if you're on a plan that exposes it.
04:28 Emma Walker: Can you demo a real-world debug: say a sudden spike in 5xxs from the model side?
04:34 Priya Kapoor: Yes — switching to the Error Analysis dashboard. You can filter to error codes, see time-series spikes, and then click into the top affected routes. The panel surfaces common prompt patterns causing failures and top N failing model variants.
04:50 Marcus Li: We also provide a root-cause suggestion engine — it says likely causes like rate-limit bursts, tokenization errors, or corrupted KV cache. It's a best-effort heuristic.
05:00 Samir Patel: Heuristics are fine as long as we can drill into raw logs.
05:04 Priya Kapoor: You can always export the matching request IDs and pull the raw payloads. There is an API to stream log slices and a Console export button.
05:15 Lydia Chen: Regarding RBAC, can we restrict who can replay vs who can see full prompts?
05:20 Alex Chen: Yes — permissions are role-based. We have scoped roles for read-only, logs-view (redacted prompts), and logs-full (full prompt visibility). SSO/SAML maps your identity provider groups to RBAC roles.
05:34 Jorge Rivera: Does audit logging capture who accessed a full prompt and when?
05:38 Alex Chen: Yes — every access event is recorded in audit logs with actor, timestamp, resource, and action. Those audit logs are also exportable for compliance.
05:46 Emma Walker: Any limitations on sampling for traces? We can't afford to trace every single request at high volume.
05:50 Priya Kapoor: We support adaptive sampling: high-fidelity traces for errors and a sampled percentage for normal traffic. You can configure rules based on route, error rate, or user-id.
06:03 Samir Patel: If we want to run a pilot with ~200 rps and target P95 below 300ms, what do you recommend for Console and log retention sizing?
06:12 Marcus Li: For that throughput, we recommend Dedicated with a single n1-standard GPU pool and enable prefix caching. Logs at 90 days is fine for initial pilot; for full production aim for 180-365 retention archived to your S3.
06:25 Alex Chen: We'll include a throughput/price worksheet after this call.
06:30 Emma Walker: Please do. Also we need to see an example of the exported NDJSON so our security team can vet it.
06:35 Priya Kapoor: I'll attach a sanitized example.
06:38 Lydia Chen: Can the Console correlate cost per request? We want cost attribution per route.
06:42 Priya Kapoor: Yes — per-request cost estimation is included if you enable token-cost attribution in the Console. We show token breakdown, model cost, and a per-route cost summary.
06:55 Jorge Rivera: One more — is there a way to set automatic rollback if a model regression crosses a quality threshold?
06:59 Marcus Li: Yes — in Rollouts you can set automated gates tied to eval suites or production metrics. If the candidate model fails, rollback happens and you get an alert.
07:10 Emma Walker: That answers most of our questions. A quick clarification — replaying doesn't count against production quotas in pilot mode, you said?
07:16 Priya Kapoor: Correct for pilot/test modes we can sandbox replays; for full prod replays count unless you route them to a test pool.
07:24 Samir Patel: Could you show how to set an alert on P95 latency and tie it to a Slack webhook?
07:29 Priya Kapoor: Sure — in Alerts you create a new rule: metric = p95 latency, scope = route or model, threshold = 300ms, timeframe = 5m. Then add a webhook destination; we have a template for Slack and Datadog.
07:44 Alex Chen: I'm going to recap next steps: I'll send the security pack and SOC2 docs; Priya will upload the screencast and NDJSON sample; Marcus will attach the throughput worksheet.
07:55 Emma Walker: Great. We'll gather sample prompts and SLOs and loop in procurement for the Dedicated pricing.
08:02 Jorge Rivera: I'll circle back with specific KMS policy questions.
08:06 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by email with the artifacts and proposed pilot timeline.
08:12 Emma Walker: Thanks all.
08:14 (meeting ends)
